subChunks.title: Ecology & the Environment

storyBeats.txt: No organism lives in isolation, Theodora said. Every species is embedded in a web of relationships — with the organisms it eats, the organisms that eat it, the organisms it competes with, and the organisms it depends on. Ecology is the science of those relationships.

The second thing to know about ecology is that energy and matter flow through ecosystems in very different ways. Energy flows in one direction — in from the sun, out as heat. Matter cycles continuously. The carbon in your body was once in the atmosphere, and will be again. The nitrogen in your proteins was fixed by bacteria in soil.

Understanding these flows is not just academic. The climate crisis is an ecology problem — carbon that was locked away for millions of years is now being cycled back into the atmosphere faster than ecosystems can absorb it. The entire biosphere is responding.

subChunks.hookHtml: Ecology is the study of interactions between organisms and their environments — including each other. From the single microhabitat of a rotting log to the global biosphere, ecological principles govern how energy flows, how nutrients cycle, how populations grow and stabilise, and how communities of species maintain (or lose) their diversity. These principles have never been more important: understanding ecology is essential to understanding and addressing the planetary-scale changes that human activity has set in motion.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Ecological Levels of Organisation

  • Individual organism
  • Population: All individuals of one species in an area — studies growth, density, age structure.
  • Community: All populations of different species in an area — studies species interactions, diversity, succession.
  • Ecosystem: Community plus its abiotic (non-living) environment — studies energy flow and nutrient cycling.
  • Biome: Large-scale ecosystems defined by climate: tropical rainforest, savanna, temperate deciduous forest, boreal forest (taiga), tundra, desert, ocean.
  • Biosphere: All ecosystems on Earth together.

Energy Flow through Ecosystems

Energy enters most ecosystems through photosynthesis by producers (autotrophs — plants, algae, cyanobacteria). This energy is then passed through trophic levels:

  • Primary producers (trophic level 1): Fix solar energy as organic molecules.
  • Primary consumers (trophic level 2): Herbivores eating producers.
  • Secondary consumers (trophic level 3): Carnivores eating herbivores.
  • Tertiary consumers (trophic level 4): Top carnivores.
  • Decomposers: Break down dead organic matter at every level — bacteria and fungi return nutrients to the ecosystem.

The 10% rule: On average, only ~10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next — the rest is lost as heat (metabolic inefficiency, respiration, uneaten material). This is why food chains rarely exceed 4–5 trophic levels (energy becomes negligibly small) and why producing meat is energetically much less efficient than eating plants directly.

Food chains depict linear feeding relationships; food webs show the full network of feeding connections in a community — much more realistic, showing the complexity of real ecosystems.

Biogeochemical Cycles

Unlike energy, matter is recycled. Key cycles:

Carbon cycle: CO₂ in atmosphere → photosynthesis (plants fix carbon) → consumption (animals eat plants) → respiration/decomposition (releases CO₂ back) → long-term storage in fossil fuels and carbonate rocks. Human burning of fossil fuels short-circuits this cycle, releasing stored carbon far faster than it is fixed.

Nitrogen cycle: Nitrogen is essential for amino acids and nucleic acids. N₂ in atmosphere is not directly usable by most organisms. Steps: nitrogen fixation (bacteria, especially Rhizobium in legume root nodules, convert N₂ to NH₃); nitrification (bacteria convert NH₃ to NO₂⁻ then NO₃⁻ — usable by plants); assimilation (plants and animals use NO₃⁻); ammonification (decomposers return nitrogen to NH₃ from dead organic matter); denitrification (bacteria return N₂ to the atmosphere).

Water (hydrological) cycle: Evaporation from oceans/land → condensation (clouds) → precipitation (rain/snow) → runoff/infiltration → evapotranspiration from plants → back to atmosphere.

Population Ecology

Exponential growth: In unlimited resources, population grows as a J-shaped curve. Rate depends on birth rate minus death rate (r, the intrinsic rate of increase).

Logistic growth: As resources become limiting, growth slows and the population stabilises at the carrying capacity (K) — the maximum population a habitat can sustain. Growth follows a S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve.

Limiting factors: Density-dependent (competition for food/space, predation, disease — stronger effect at high density) vs density-independent (climate events, fires — regardless of population density).

Species Interactions

  • Competition (−/−): Both species harmed; for resources.
  • Predation (+/−): Predator benefits; prey harmed. Drives co-evolution (prey defences; predator counter-adaptations).
  • Mutualism (+/+): Both benefit: bees and flowers; lichens (fungi + algae); mycorrhizal fungi + plant roots.
  • Commensalism (+/0): One benefits; other unaffected: barnacles on whales.
  • Parasitism (+/−): Parasite benefits; host harmed: tapeworms, mistletoe.

Biodiversity and Conservation

Biodiversity has three levels: genetic (variation within species), species (number and abundance of species), and ecosystem diversity. Higher biodiversity generally increases ecosystem resilience and productivity. The current sixth mass extinction — driven by habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, and climate change — is eliminating species at estimated rates 100–1,000× the background extinction rate.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why it takes roughly 10 kilograms of plants to produce 1 kilogram of cow — and what this means for the efficiency of different diets.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml: A grassland ecosystem has the following food chain: grass → grasshoppers → frogs → herons. (1) At which trophic level is each organism? (2) If the grass fixes 100,000 kJ of energy per year, approximately how much energy is available to the herons? (3) A pesticide is applied that kills grasshoppers. Predict the short-term and long-term effects on the frog and heron populations. (4) A new species of grass-eating vole is introduced. Predict how this changes the food web and what might happen to the grasshopper population, using the concept of competitive exclusion or niche partitioning.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
(1) Grass: producer/trophic level 1. Grasshoppers: primary consumers/trophic level 2. Frogs: secondary consumers/trophic level 3. Herons: tertiary consumers/trophic level 4.

(2) Using the 10% rule: grass 100,000 kJ → grasshoppers receive 10,000 kJ (10%) → frogs receive 1,000 kJ (10%) → herons receive 100 kJ (10%). Herons have access to approximately 100 kJ — only 0.1% of original energy. This is why top predators are rare relative to producers.

(3) Short-term: grasshopper population crashes → frogs lose their prey, frog population declines → with fewer frogs to eat, heron population also declines (delayed, because herons may switch prey). Long-term: with fewer grasshopper herbivores, grass may initially grow unchecked (competitive release). If frogs decline significantly, herons may shift to alternative prey or decline further. The food web becomes destabilised — species that previously relied on grasshoppers as intermediaries face food shortages. If grasshoppers do not recover, frog populations may collapse, affecting herons and indirectly affecting grass abundance.

(4) The introduced voles compete with grasshoppers for grass (competition at trophic level 2 for the same resource). Two outcomes are possible: (a) Competitive exclusion: if voles are more efficient at exploiting the grass resource, they could outcompete grasshoppers and eliminate them from the ecosystem (Gause's principle: two species cannot coexist indefinitely on identical resources). (b) Niche partitioning: if voles and grasshoppers exploit slightly different aspects of the grass resource (different plant parts, different times of day, different microhabitats), they can coexist by dividing the niche. In either case, frogs now have an additional potential prey item (voles), which might buffer the frog population if grasshoppers decline due to competition.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Explain why the global nitrogen cycle is essential for life on Earth, and why human disruption of this cycle through industrial agriculture poses ecological risks. Your answer should include: (1) why nitrogen is limiting for life; (2) how natural nitrogen fixation works and why it is significant; (3) how the Haber-Bosch process changed food production; (4) the ecological consequences of reactive nitrogen accumulation in ecosystems (eutrophication, dead zones, nitrous oxide emissions).
subChunks.modelAnswer:
(1) Nitrogen is essential because it is a component of amino acids (the building blocks of all proteins) and nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). Plants and animals cannot use atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) directly — the triple bond in N₂ is extremely strong and requires significant energy to break. This makes biologically available (reactive) nitrogen a limiting nutrient for plant growth in many ecosystems. Without a steady supply of reactive nitrogen, photosynthesis and plant growth are constrained, which limits all life higher in the food web.

(2) Natural nitrogen fixation is performed by specialised bacteria (diazotrophs): free-living bacteria such as Azotobacter in soil, and symbiotic bacteria such as Rhizobium in root nodules of leguminous plants (clover, peas, beans, acacias). These bacteria possess the enzyme nitrogenase, which converts N₂ to ammonia (NH₃) using substantial energy (16 ATP per N₂). The fixed nitrogen is then available to plants. Historically, this biological nitrogen fixation was the primary input of reactive nitrogen into terrestrial ecosystems, keeping reactive nitrogen a scarce and therefore growth-limiting resource — which in turn controlled ecosystem productivity and biodiversity.

(3) The Haber-Bosch process (Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch, ~1909–1913) industrially synthesises ammonia by reacting N₂ with H₂ under high temperature and pressure using an iron catalyst: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. This made nitrogen fertiliser available on a massive scale. Estimates suggest Haber-Bosch nitrogen fertiliser supports the food supply of roughly half the current global human population — it is the single largest reason why Earth can support 8 billion people today. The process also consumes ~1–2% of global energy and generates significant CO₂.

(4) Ecological consequences of reactive nitrogen accumulation: (a) Eutrophication — excess nitrogen from agricultural runoff enters water bodies, stimulating explosive algal growth (algal blooms). When the algae die and decompose, bacterial decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen, creating hypoxic (oxygen-depleted) "dead zones" where fish and invertebrates cannot survive. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone (created by Mississippi River agricultural runoff) is a large-scale example. (b) Dead zones — hypoxic or anoxic zones in coastal waters and lakes caused by eutrophication; significantly reduce aquatic biodiversity. (c) Nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions — bacterial denitrification of excess agricultural nitrogen produces N₂O, a greenhouse gas approximately 298× more potent than CO₂ per molecule over 100 years, and a major ozone-depleting substance. Agricultural nitrogen use is the largest anthropogenic source of N₂O. (d) Soil acidification — nitrification produces acid, lowering soil pH and leaching cations. (e) Biodiversity loss — nitrogen enrichment of grasslands and heathlands favours fast-growing species (especially grasses) that outcompete rare, slow-growing specialists adapted to low-nitrogen conditions.
learningObjectives: Describe energy flow through trophic levels and explain why energy transfer is typically only ~10% efficient between levels.
Outline the carbon and nitrogen cycles, identifying key processes and organisms at each step.
Distinguish exponential from logistic population growth and explain the role of carrying capacity and limiting factors.
Describe the five types of species interaction (competition, predation, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism) with examples.
commonMistakes: Thinking the 10% rule means 10% of animals in a population are transferred — the 10% refers to energy, not organisms or biomass count.
Confusing decomposers with consumers in a food chain — decomposers break down dead organic matter at all levels; they are not part of the linear producer-consumer chain.
Stating that matter is lost from ecosystems as it moves up food chains — matter cycles; only energy is lost (as heat) at each trophic transfer.
Treating carrying capacity as a fixed maximum — carrying capacity (K) changes with environmental conditions and resource availability.
assessmentCriteria: Correctly applies the 10% rule to calculate energy available at higher trophic levels from a given primary production value.
Accurately describes at least three steps of the nitrogen cycle with the microorganisms involved.
Predicts population and community responses to a perturbation (species removal, introduction, or resource change) using ecological principles.
Explains eutrophication mechanistically — from excess nitrogen input to hypoxic dead zone formation.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The indirect effects that reverberate through a food web when a top predator is added or removed — e.g., reintroduction of wolves in Yellowstone changed elk behaviour, allowing vegetation to recover, changing river courses; demonstrates how predators shape entire ecosystems.

A species with a disproportionately large effect on ecosystem structure and function relative to its biomass — e.g., sea otters (control sea urchin populations, which would otherwise devastate kelp forests).

Nutrient (especially nitrogen and phosphorus) enrichment of a water body, stimulating algal growth; subsequent decomposition of dead algae depletes dissolved oxygen, creating hypoxic dead zones that kill fish and invertebrates.

Industrial synthesis of ammonia from N₂ and H₂ (1909–1913); responsible for nitrogen fertilisers that support ~half the global food supply but have dramatically increased reactive nitrogen in ecosystems, driving eutrophication and N₂O emissions.

The current, ongoing extinction event driven by human activity (habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, climate change); estimated extinction rates are 100–1,000× background rates.

questions.questionHtml: Why do food chains typically have no more than four or five trophic levels?
options: Top predators are too large to eat anything above them
The 10% energy transfer efficiency means that very little energy remains at higher trophic levels — by level 5, less than 0.01% of the original energy is available
Ecosystems can only support four or five species
Larger predators reproduce too slowly to maintain a population
questions.correctAnswer: The 10% energy transfer efficiency means that very little energy remains at higher trophic levels — by level 5, less than 0.01% of the original energy is available
questions.explanationHtml: With ~10% transfer efficiency per level: producers (100%) → primary consumers (10%) → secondary (1%) → tertiary (0.1%) → quaternary (0.01%). By trophic level 5, only 0.01% of the original solar energy fixed by producers remains. There is simply not enough energy to support a viable population at a 6th trophic level. This is why apex predators are always rare relative to producers, and why large carnivores require vast territories.

questions.questionHtml: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules convert atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) to ammonia (NH₃). Why is this process essential for most plants and animals?
options: Because N₂ is toxic and must be converted before plants can grow near it
Because most organisms cannot break the strong N≡N triple bond in N₂ — they can only use reactive forms of nitrogen (NH₃, NO₃⁻) for making amino acids and nucleotides
Because nitrogen fixation releases energy that plants use for photosynthesis
Because NH₃ prevents soil acidification, allowing plants to absorb water
questions.correctAnswer: Because most organisms cannot break the strong N≡N triple bond in N₂ — they can only use reactive forms of nitrogen (NH₃, NO₃⁻) for making amino acids and nucleotides
questions.explanationHtml: The N≡N triple bond has a bond energy of 945 kJ/mol — among the strongest in chemistry. Only nitrogen-fixing bacteria possess the enzyme nitrogenase (which requires ~16 ATP per N₂ fixed) to break this bond and produce ammonia. Ammonia and nitrate are the reactive nitrogen forms plants can absorb through roots and use to synthesise amino acids, proteins, and nucleic acids. Without biological nitrogen fixation, reactive nitrogen would be scarce and most ecosystems would be severely nitrogen-limited.

questions.questionHtml: Bees are pollinators that help flowering plants reproduce, while also collecting nectar for food. The plant gains pollination; the bee gains nectar. What type of species interaction is this, and why does it differ from parasitism even though the bee is consuming plant resources?
options: Parasitism — the bee harms the plant by taking its nectar
Commensalism — only the bee benefits; the plant is unaffected
Mutualism — both species benefit (plant gains pollination and reproduction; bee gains nectar as food). It differs from parasitism because the plant benefits rather than being harmed
Competition — both species compete for the same floral resources
questions.correctAnswer: Mutualism — both species benefit (plant gains pollination and reproduction; bee gains nectar as food). It differs from parasitism because the plant benefits rather than being harmed
questions.explanationHtml: Mutualism (+/+): both species benefit. The plant produces nectar as an evolutionary 'payment' for pollination services — a small energy investment that enables reproduction. The bee gets food. Parasitism (+/−) would require the bee to harm the plant's fitness — but here the plant's reproductive success depends on the bee. The bee-flower relationship has co-evolved: flower shape, colour, and scent have evolved to attract specific pollinators; bee tongues and pollen-carrying structures have evolved to match flowers. This co-evolution demonstrates the mutualistic relationship.
